content: In the anatomy of the female reproductive system, the canal of the cervix, also referred to as the endocervical canal, cervical canal, cervical canal of the uterus, or the cavity of the cervix, is a spindle-shaped, flattened passageway located within the cervix, which is the neck of the uterus. This canal connects the uterine cavity to the vagina. It communicates with the uterine cavity through the internal orifice of the uterus and with the vagina through the external orifice. The walls of the cervical canal feature an anterior and a posterior longitudinal ridge. From each of these ridges, several small oblique columns extend, forming structures known as the palmate folds. These folds resemble branches stemming from the trunk of a tree, and this arrangement is referred to as the arbor vitae uteri (Latin for tree of life of the uterus). The folds on the anterior and posterior walls of the canal are not perfectly aligned with one another. Instead, they interlock in a way that effectively closes the cervical canal.
